cards.title: Speed up a Shopify store by minifying CSS/JS
cards.summary: Remove whitespace, line breaks and comments from CSS/JS to cut file size and speed up page load.
cards.use_when: When auditing storefront page speed and deciding whether technical asset optimisation is worth the effort before other work.
steps: Understand the principle: browsers don't need the spacing, line breaks and comments developers add for readability, so removing them shrinks files without changing functionality.
For a manual route, run JavaScript through a JS compressor and CSS through a CSS minifier.

Shopify gives a built-in option: name CSS files with the .css.liquid extension and Shopify minifies them automatically — verify the current accepted file extension in Shopify's docs before relying on this.
For non-developers, an app such as File Optimizer can automate minification of JS and CSS files.
Recommend getting a developer involved if you are not confident, because broken scripts can break cart or product functionality.
caveats: The source presents minification as one part of a broader speed playbook; it is not claimed to be sufficient alone.
Test on a duplicate theme before pushing live.

cards.title: Async and defer non-essential scripts
cards.summary: Load chat widgets, analytics and tracking scripts asynchronously or deferred so the page renders and becomes interactive sooner.
cards.use_when: When third-party scripts (live chat, analytics, tracking pixels) are blocking rendering and hurting storefront speed.
steps: Classify each script: non-essential scripts are those that don't affect core site functionality — live chat widgets, analytics and tracking tags are the source's examples.
For asynchronous loading, add the async attribute to the script tag; the script downloads in parallel and executes as soon as possible.
For deferred loading, add the defer attribute; the script downloads in parallel but executes after the main content has parsed.
Both approaches let the page render and become interactive faster by moving non-critical script work out of the critical path.
Have a developer implement this carefully and test checkout, cart and product-page interactions afterwards to confirm nothing breaks.
caveats: The source says this should be done carefully, preferably by a developer, to avoid negative impact on site functionality.
Do not defer scripts that the cart, variant picker or checkout depends on.

cards.title: Use resource hints and preload to cut load times
cards.summary: Add preload, prefetch, DNS-prefetch and preconnect link elements in the head to control how and when key resources load.
cards.use_when: When optimising storefront load speed for above-the-fold assets, next-page navigation, or third-party domains like analytics and social buttons.
steps: Add a link element with the appropriate rel attribute and the resource URL, placed in the head of the HTML so it is acted upon early in page load.
Use preload for resources needed immediately on the current page (for example a hero image or critical font).
Use prefetch for resources needed for future pages, which makes subsequent navigation snappier.
Use DNS-prefetch and preconnect for third-party resources you know will be used, such as analytics or social media buttons.
Verify the exact syntax in current Shopify theme documentation before editing, since theme structure and supported tags can change.
caveats: The source describes implementation as fairly simple but the actual edits sit in theme code and need testing.
Resource hints are one part of site speed, not a fix for heavy images or bloated apps.

cards.title: Frame keyword research around customer thought process, not just volume
cards.summary: Keyword research is uncovering the search terms people use when looking for your products, services or information — it maps the customer's thought process.
cards.use_when: When planning which collections, product pages and blog posts to build or optimise for organic search on a Shopify store.
steps: Start from a seed product term (the source's example is blackout curtains) and ask what a real customer would type, not what you would call the product.
Generate variations across dimensions: material (linen blackout curtains), room (blackout curtains for bedroom), question form (do blackout curtains keep heat out), and buyer vs explorer phrasing.
Recognise that each variation can attract a different audience or indicate a different stage of the buying journey.
Use the research to decide which pages to prioritise, which questions to answer with content, and what competitors are already targeting.
Expect the output to serve four things: more long-tail visibility, more relevant traffic, better conversion from high-buyer-intent terms, and a sharper content strategy.
caveats: The source stresses that rankings and search volume alone are not the point; search intent understanding is.
No specific volume thresholds are given.

cards.title: Build a topical map instead of a flat keyword list
cards.summary: A topical map is keyword research extended into a roadmap of every topic and page needed to be seen as the authority in your niche.
cards.use_when: When a store has scattered SEO pages and you need a single plan for which collections, subcollections and blog posts should exist.
steps: Understand the goal: outline every topic you need to cover to be recognised as the leading expert in your industry, not just a list of keywords.
Pull the matching keywords for your seed topic from a tool such as Semrush — the source's example found roughly 21,000 keywords containing 'blackout curtain' — and note their volumes and difficulty.

Cluster keywords by search intent so you know which group of terms can be served by one page rather than many; the source recommends Keyword Cupid for automatic clustering based on SERP similarity, or you can cluster manually.
Prioritise by volume, then move the highest-volume clusters into a keyword map that lists keyword, volume, and cluster.
In a second tab (the topical map), assign each cluster a page type — collection, product or blog post — plus a primary keyword, secondary keywords, URL, volume, current rankings and status.
Track publication status and, for published pages, whether each needs a content refresh, a quick-win optimisation, or no change.
Use additional sources such as Wikipedia, Google Trends, competitor sites and Exploding Topics to find topics you missed.
caveats: The presenter uses this as their own preferred method and says it is 'keyword research on steroids'; it is not the only valid approach.
Keyword Cupid and Semrush are the tools the source names; interfaces and pricing change, so verify current features.

cards.title: Decide page type by what ranks in positions 1–3
cards.summary: Match your target page type (collection, product, or blog post) to the content type Google already rewards for that keyword.
cards.use_when: When a keyword cluster could plausibly be served by a collection page, a product page or a blog post and you need to choose.
steps: Search the keyword and inspect what type of pages occupy the top three results.
If the top three are collection pages (as with 'blackout curtains'), target the keyword with a collection page.
If the results are informational articles (as with 'blackout curtain alternatives'), target the keyword with a blog post.
If results are mixed, lean toward whatever occupies positions 1–3, because that is where you want to be and Google is signalling the content type it wants.

Then apply the buyer's perspective: someone searching a broad category term probably wants options (collection page), while a very specific query like a product name, size, or unusual feature combination suggests a specific product (product page).
Note that very specific product-page keywords may have little to no search volume, which raises the separate question of whether those pages are worth indexing at all.
caveats: The source calls deciding page type 'a little tricky'; intent is the deciding factor, not a fixed rule.
Google's SERPs shift over time, so re-check before committing a build.

cards.title: Prioritise bottom-of-funnel pages first on Shopify
cards.summary: Start SEO with collection and product pages, because they lead directly to revenue and pay back fastest.
cards.use_when: When deciding what to optimise first across hundreds of existing collection and product pages.
steps: Rank page priorities in this order: bottom-of-funnel pages (collections and products) first, blog posts later, because bottom-of-funnel pages lead to revenue growth and let you see return on the SEO effort sooner.
Within those pages, open Google Search Console and sort by number of impressions to find low-hanging fruit — pages already close to the top three where a visibility improvement could convert quickly.

Look for the small subtopics where search engines already treat you as an authority; these pages tend to receive the most impressions, and optimising them plus closely related pages moves the needle faster than switching to an unrelated collection.
Pair that with a Keyword Gap analysis: enter your domain plus a few competitors, and review the keywords competitors rank for that you don't.

If your backlink profile is stronger than the competitor's, the source argues you should be able to outrank them on those gap terms — this is most powerful for well-established brands with strong link profiles.
caveats: The prioritisation rationale is the presenter's experience, not a measured benchmark.
Keyword Gap relies on backlink-profile strength; a weaker-profile store should not assume it can outrank the competitor.

cards.title: One topic per page, many secondary keywords per page
cards.summary: Cluster a primary keyword with its close variants on one page, and split genuinely different topics onto separate pages.
cards.use_when: When mapping keywords to URLs so one page can rank for many terms without competing against your own pages.
steps: Set one primary keyword per page — it goes in the H1, the URL and the title tag.

Add secondary keywords that are variations of, or closely related to, the primary keyword: singular/plural variants, common misspellings (the source's example is 'block out curtains'), and attribute variants that would still be served by the same page and product set.
Split topics that would clearly show different products: white blackout curtains and pink blackout curtains should not share a page because they require different product results.

Cluster manually, or use a tool such as Keyword Cupid, which the source says clusters based on the Google algorithm — if the SERPs for two keywords are similar, it clusters them together, removing the guesswork.
Remember the rule is one topic per page, not one keyword per page; a single page legitimately ranks for many keywords.
caveats: Cluster tools are only as good as their SERP data and change over time.
The source states this as its own operating rule for Shopify stores, not as a Google-documented requirement.

cards.title: Assign URL types: collections for options, products for specifics, homepage for breadth
cards.summary: Collection pages capture broad transactional terms, product pages capture highly specific ones, and the homepage targets broad high-level keywords.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether a keyword should live on a collection, a product page, or the homepage.
steps: Assign to collection pages the transactional and option-seeking terms: brand names, features, colours, materials, styles — anything where the searcher wants a variety of choices.
Assign to product pages only truly specific queries, e.g. a combination like 'aqua blue room darkening curtains' that signals a specific product; size and niche feature searches also fit here.
Accept that collection pages will usually outconvert product pages for broad terms, because a collection offering many options better matches what the searcher wants.
Use the homepage for broad, high-level keywords (the source's curtain-shop example is 'buy curtains online'), while individual collections cover narrower categories.

Check for cannibalisation: make sure the homepage keyword isn't also the target of a collection page (a bicycle store using 'buy bicycles online' on the homepage should not also target it with a collection).
caveats: The source notes it is debatable whether highly specific product pages with no search volume are worth indexing at all, and that some stores may be better off pushing crawl toward collections.
The source argues there is no SEO problem with reusing the same products across multiple collections when it makes sense to users.

cards.title: Derive site structure and internal links from the topical map
cards.summary: A clean topical map becomes a site structure of homepage, collections and subcollections that mirrors how search engines expect topics to relate.
cards.use_when: When building or restructuring catalogue hierarchy and internal links for a Shopify store.
steps: Take the topical map and turn it into a hierarchy: homepage at the top, then primary collections (e.g. blackout curtains, sheer curtains, lace curtains, kitchen curtains), then subcollections under a parent.
Create subcollections by attribute — by room (blackout curtains for bedroom), by material (linen blackout curtains), by colour (white blackout curtains).
Treat each collection page as dedicated to one specific product category and one specific topic, so pages stay unique from one another.
Use the mental model that a search query is a question and your page is an answer; the easier you make the question-to-answer match, the higher you are likely to rank.

Feature subcollections inside their parent collection pages — the source's example is MyProtein's whey protein page linking to dairy-free protein, clear protein drinks and protein blends — which improves navigation and makes the hierarchy easy for search engines to crawl.
Note that Shopify has no native subcollection feature; you create a new collection and treat it as a subcollection.
caveats: Crawl-depth guidance ('lower depth is better') comes from studies the source cites generally, not from a specific controlled test.
Restructuring URLs on a live store needs redirect planning, which this section does not cover.

cards.title: Spot and fix keyword cannibalisation
cards.summary: Cannibalisation is multiple pages on your site competing for the same keyword, which confuses search engines about which page to rank.
cards.use_when: When a collection, product or blog page isn't ranking as expected and you suspect competing pages on the same store.
steps: Check for overlapping targets: a collection page and a product page both targeting the same keyword (e.g. both targeting 'blackout curtains') is a cannibalisation problem.
Check content redundancy: blog posts targeting keywords already covered by collection pages.
Check keyword overuse — spreading the same keyword across many pages on the assumption it improves rankings, which the source says actually confuses search engines.
Fix by applying one page per topic: give each page one primary keyword and split overlapping pages into distinct, genuinely different topics rather than near-duplicates.
Keep secondary keywords on each page so you still capture variants without creating new competing pages.

Also look for near-duplicate collection ideas: pages like 'top rated gardening tools', 'most popular gardening tools' and 'gardening tools on sale' will compete for the same keywords and offer no unique value.
caveats: The failure mode described (internal competition confusing search engines) is the source's explanation; it is not framed as a documented ranking factor.
Merging or deleting pages affects existing traffic — check Search Console data before removing URLs.

cards.title: Expand broad topics into subcollections without creating redundancy
cards.summary: Splitting a broad category into focused subcollections captures more search entry points, but only where each page has a genuinely distinct offer.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to break a large collection into subcollections or keep it as one page.
steps: Create as many genuinely distinct collections and subcollections as the catalogue supports, because each one is an additional search entry point and increases total addressable market.
Split by meaningful dimensions: for a vacuum collection, the source suggests stick, upright, handheld and robotic vacuums.
Use a 'shop by' menu structure (by size, type, colour, feature) as a brainstorming device for which collections and subcollections your brand could have.
Use keyword tools such as Semrush to confirm the splits have search demand: enter the main keyword (e.g. vacuum cleaner) and review the containing keywords with difficulty and monthly volume.

Reuse products across multiple collections where it makes sense to users — the source says a cordless vacuum and a stick vacuum collection can both legitimately contain the same product without SEO problems.
Do not create near-duplicate pages (e.g. three 'best/top/sale gardening tools' pages); those compete with each other and add no unique value.
caveats: The source does not give a numeric threshold for when a category is broad enough to split; it describes the expand-vs-consolidate line as thin and requiring judgement.
The 'over 80% of organic revenue from collection pages for stores with 50+ products' figure is the presenter's stated generalisation, not a measured benchmark for your store.

cards.title: Stick to your core topic and avoid diluting relevance
cards.summary: Publishing content far outside your topical map dilutes the site's perceived expertise and can cost rankings on core topics.
cards.use_when: When considering a new category, blog theme, or shoulder niche that sits outside your store's existing topic focus.
steps: Map how close a new topic sits to your core in Google's knowledge graph: blackout curtains, sheer curtains and linen curtains are close together; tablecloths are noticeably further; an unrelated category is furthest.
Keep publishing inside the topical map where every piece of content reinforces authority on the subjects you have chosen to cover.

Treat the source's warning as a live risk, not theoretical: the presenter describes a site that dominated a niche, expanded into shoulder niches, ranked briefly for a few months, and then lost rankings — search engines recrawled the site, judged it no longer sticking to its core competencies, and rankings dropped for the main topic too, not just the new one.
Before expanding, ask whether the new content would confuse both users and search engines about the site's actual purpose.
If expanding, do it only after the core topical map is maximally covered.
caveats: This is a practitioner's account of one overexpansion experience, not a controlled study or a promise about any specific site.
The 'few months' timeline and the loss of core rankings are specific to that case.

cards.title: Optimise the main menu for fewer clicks to product
cards.summary: Match main-menu structure to catalogue size: minimal for small stores, direct subcategory access for large, shop-by-x for varied ranges.
cards.use_when: When designing or revising the storefront main navigation to improve usability and crawl efficiency.
steps: For small catalogues with few product categories, a simple 'Shop' menu may be sufficient — the source's example is an outdoor brand using a single 'shop gear' entry that routes to core collections.

For large catalogues with many categories (protein, bestsellers, creatine, amino acids, pre-workout), give direct menu access to subcategories like whey, clear, vegan and blended protein so users don't have to click through a parent first.

For stores with varied collections — by brand, style or goal — use a 'shop by x' navigation directly in the main menu; the source's example offers blinds by type, colour, window type, room and feature.
Set the goal as minimising the number of clicks needed to reach a desired product for both users and search engines.
Keep in mind the two stated benefits: better user experience (lower bounce, higher conversion) and SEO benefits (crawl efficiency, link equity distribution, reduced crawl depth).
caveats: The claim that lower crawl depth typically means better rankings is attributed to studies in general, not to a controlled test by the source.
Menu complexity can hurt mobile usability — the source does not address mobile specifics.

cards.title: Make the homepage a hub for high-volume collections
cards.summary: Feature your highest-search-volume collection pages prominently at the top of the homepage to serve users and push backlink equity into money pages.
cards.use_when: When designing homepage layout and choosing which collections to surface first.
steps: Identify which collection pages have the highest search volume — those likely reflect what your audience is most interested in.
Feature them prominently at the top of the homepage using banners or featured sections so they are instantly accessible.
Aim for as few clicks as possible from homepage to those collections.
Add engaging content or promotions around those featured collections to draw attention.

Understand the SEO logic: the homepage usually has the most backlinks and is the most visited page, so linking out to high-volume collections passes backlink equity to pages whose ranking potential you want to improve.
Study the source's example: a blinds retailer whose homepage essentially mirrors its main menu, with shop-by-type, shop-by-colour, most-popular and shop-by-room sections.
caveats: The link-equity distribution rationale is standard SEO reasoning presented by the source, not a measured result from a test.
Don't overload the homepage to the point of slowing load time.

cards.title: Handle faceted navigation correctly on Shopify
cards.summary: Default Shopify filter URLs are parameter-based and are not indexed, so keyword-targeted filters need their own dedicated collection pages.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to add filters to a collection page and whether those filters should rank for anything.
steps: Decide whether faceted navigation is needed at all: a store with a few products likely doesn't need it, while a store with hundreds or thousands of SKUs likely does.

Understand the default: most Shopify themes use URL parameters for filters, and those parameter URLs are not indexed by search engines, which simplifies the site structure but means filtered pages won't rank for specific keywords.
If you want to target a specific keyword inside a filter dimension, manually create a dedicated collection page for it.
Treat that manual creation as a benefit, not a workaround: a dedicated collection lets you add unique content and customise the page, which a parameter-filtered view cannot.
Choose which filter dimensions to offer based on what helps customers narrow down (size, colour, price; the source's example uses food texture, flavour, special diet and life stage).
caveats: This describes default Shopify theme behaviour; confirm how your specific theme and apps handle filter URLs before assuming filters won't index.
The source frames faceted navigation mainly as a large-catalogue tool.

cards.title: Build product grids for both users and crawlers
cards.summary: Avoid JavaScript-loaded product grids, show 36–48 products per page, and put useful product details directly in the grid.
cards.use_when: When setting up or redesigning collection page product grids on a Shopify store.
steps: Do not load product grids with JavaScript — the source says search engines typically struggle to crawl JavaScript content efficiently; use the default Shopify Search & Discovery app to generate grids instead.
Show roughly 36 to 48 products per page, aiming for as many as possible without compromising site speed, to avoid excessive pagination (the source's example is 21 pages for one collection).

Use numbered pagination rather than previous/next controls, because users and crawlers cannot skip to a specific page otherwise — the source notes some stores only offer next/previous, which forces multiple clicks to reach page five.
Add product details into the grid — colour options, a short description, size, pickup or delivery — so customers can decide without clicking through to the product page.
Treat the added detail as both a UX improvement and extra page content, which the source says adds relevance and usually leads to higher rankings.
Add faceted navigation for brands with heavy SKU counts (the source's benchmark: roughly 200 SKUs means customers will struggle to find items without filters).
caveats: The 36–48 figure is the presenter's recommendation, explicitly conditioned on not slowing the site.
The SKU/collection relationship ('over 50 products → collections drive 80%+ of organic revenue') is the source's generalisation, not a measured statistic for your store.

cards.title: Add breadcrumbs, tag-style links and related products to product pages
cards.summary: Use three internal-link patterns on product pages to strengthen navigation, distribute link equity and aid discovery.
cards.use_when: When auditing product page template and internal linking on a Shopify store.
steps: Add breadcrumbs that give a clear path back to broader categories; the source notes most Shopify themes include this by default, so check whether yours does.

Add tag-style category links that let shoppers explore related collections and products — the source's example is a fishing tackle product page linking to vertical jigs, ice fishing jigs, blade baits, shown near the product description.
Add a related products section to boost sales and reduce navigation clicks; the source's example is Amazon's related-products row.
Recognise the combined SEO effect: these patterns distribute link equity more effectively and improve discoverability across the product range.
Treat this as often underused on Shopify stores hosting thousands of products, where effective linking on product pages meaningfully improves site structure.
caveats: Shopify theme support varies, so verify whether breadcrumbs and tag-style links are native or need code/apps.
The source presents the sales lift from related products as a benefit rather than citing a measured uplift.

cards.title: Optimise the three key on-page elements on collection pages
cards.summary: Title tag, URL and H1 are the first elements search engines crawl and the strongest signal of what the page is about.
cards.use_when: When writing or rewriting collection page metadata for a Shopify store.
steps: Place the target keyword as close to the start of the title tag as possible — if the target is 'vegan protein powder', lead with that phrase.
Use up to roughly 60 characters in the title tag; if you aren't near 60, add secondary keywords or modifiers like 'buy online' or 'shop', or longer-tail variants of the target keyword.
Set the H1 to the target keyword itself — 'vegan protein powder' as the H1 if that is the target.
Keep the URL as short as possible and mirror the target keyword — the source's direction is simply 'vegan protein powder' as the slug.
Remember the broader principle: one page per topic, one primary keyword per page plus secondary keywords.
caveats: The ~60 character guidance is presented as a working rule of thumb, not a hard limit enforced by Google.
Shopify auto-generates some of these fields, so check for template overrides.

cards.title: Decide what to do with a page: publish, refresh, or quick-win
cards.summary: Track each mapped topic's publication and performance status so the topical map becomes an actionable worklist rather than a document.
cards.use_when: When turning a completed keyword/topical map into a prioritised production and optimisation queue.
steps: Build a keyword map first that lists keywords with their search volumes, then cluster them.
Carry each cluster into the topical map tab and assign: primary keyword, secondary keywords, page type (collection, product or blog post), URL, main keyword volume, and current ranking.
Mark whether the page is published or not.
For published pages, record the decision: needs a content refresh, leave as is, or apply SEO quick wins.
For unpublished pages, the goal is simply to publish that piece of content.
Keep the two tabs separate — keyword map for research, topical map for the live plan — so volume prioritisation stays visible while you work.
caveats: The source describes its own template workflow; the specific columns are the presenter's structure, not a standard.
The template link is referenced in the original training material.
